title: Unitree, China’s humanoid robot champion, lists in Shanghai on 19 August after record demand
excerpt: Unitree Robotics is due to debut on Shanghai’s STAR Market on 19 August at close to a $9bn valuation, having raised about 6.1bn yuan.
content_html:
Unitree Robotics, the Hangzhou company that has done more than anyone else to turn Chinese humanoid robots into a spectator sport, is due to begin trading on Shanghai’s STAR Market on 19 August, according to Reuters.

The listing makes it the first general-purpose humanoid maker to go public on the mainland, and it arrives having already cleared the paperwork: China’s securities regulator signed off on the registration earlier in the year, when the numbers looked far more modest.

Unitree priced its shares at 150.8 yuan apiece, selling roughly 40mn new shares, about a tenth of the enlarged company, to raise some 6.1bn yuan, or around $900mn.

That values the business at close to 61bn yuan, near $9bn, comfortably above the 42bn yuan the market had pencilled in only weeks earlier and well beyond the $7bn figure floated during the run-up.

For a firm that was barely a household name a few years ago, and one that still sells more robot dogs than androids, it is a startling repricing.

Retail investors oversubscribed the offer by more than 8,000 times, a record for the STAR Market, and the overall book was covered several thousand times over, leaving an allocation rate of roughly 0.018 percent.

Grey-market pricing has pointed to first-day gains of triple to quadruple the offer price, which is less a valuation than a mood. Chinese new listings returned an average of 233 percent on debut in the first half of 2026, so exuberance is, for now, simply the baseline.

Also, on Monday, two days before the float and timed to the opening of the World Robot Conference in Beijing, Unitree unveiled a new high-speed humanoid nicknamed “Superman”, built, it says, in little over three months and able to jump two metres from standing and hit 12.66 metres per second, quicker over the ground than Usain Bolt at his peak.

Video: Unitree Robotics / YouTube

The company freely calls it a work in progress; it also, conveniently, handed investors one more viral clip to pass around in the days before pricing.

What is being bought, underneath the theatre, is real enough. Unitree made its name on nimble quadruped robot dogs before moving into bipeds, and its G1 and H-series humanoids are now fixtures of the internet’s robot-video economy, running, dancing, sparring and picking themselves up after a shove.

The founder, Wang Xingxing, still only in his mid-thirties, holds about a third of the company and is, on paper, China’s first humanoid-robot billionaire; backers include Tencent, Alibaba and the AI upstart DeepSeek.

The financial picture is more nuanced than the queue outside the offering suggests. Revenue has more than quadrupled year on year, and Unitree, unusually for the sector, has been profitable for several years.

Yet its first-quarter net profit fell sharply, by close to half depending on the filing, as research and marketing spending climbed, the familiar shape of a company sprinting to stay ahead of a crowded field rather than coasting on fat margins.

It is also, unmistakably, a national project. Beijing has thrown its weight behind humanoids as a strategic industry, and the debut is read at home as a milestone for Chinese hardware rather than a mere corporate event.

Competition is thickening accordingly, with rivals such as AgiBot, Leju and EngineAI chasing their own listings in Hong Kong and Shenzhen, and whether any can turn viral demonstrations into durable businesses is another matter, on distinctly mixed early evidence.

For all the theatre, the underlying question remains unresolved. Unitree makes machines that can somersault; it has yet to prove that it can somersault into a mass market where buyers stay satisfied and orders recur.

Even Nvidia, whose chips power much of this boom, has been quietly spreading its bets across other robot makers. I

nvestors bidding the stock up thousands of times over are wagering that the demonstrations are a prologue. From 19 August, the market will start, cautiously or otherwise, to find out.

content_html_zh:
据路透社报道，杭州公司 Unitree Robotics 将于 8 月 19 日开始在上海科创板交易，该公司在将中国人形机器人变成一项观赏性运动方面所做的努力比其他任何公司都多。

这次上市使其成为第一家在大陆上市的通用人形机器人制造商，而且它已经完成了所有手续：中国证券监管机构在今年早些时候批准了注册，当时的数字看起来要小得多。

UniTree将其股票定价为每股150.8元人民币，发行了约4000万股新股，约占扩大后公司的十分之一，筹集了约61亿元人民币（约合9亿美元）。

该业务的估值接近 610 亿元人民币，接近 90 亿美元，远高于市场几周前预测的 420 亿元人民币，也远高于上涨期间的 70 亿美元。

对于一家几年前还算家喻户晓、机器狗销量仍多于机器人的公司来说，这是一次令人震惊的重新定价。

散户超额认购超过8000倍，创科创板纪录，整体认购数达数千倍，分配率约为0.018%。

灰市定价表明首日涨幅是要约价格的三到四倍，这与其说是估值，不如说是一种情绪。 2026 年上半年，中国新上市公司上市时的平均回报率为 233%，因此目前的繁荣程度只是基线。

此外，周一，即花车活动前两天，恰逢北京世界机器人大会开幕，Unitree 推出了一款绰号为“超人”的新型高速人形机器人，据称该机器人在三个月多一点的时间里建成，能够从站立处跳跃两米，每秒达到 12.66 米，比巅峰时期的尤塞恩·博尔特 (Usain Bolt) 更快。

视频：Unitree Robotics / YouTube

该公司自由地将其称为“正在进行的工作”；它还方便地向投资者提供了一个在定价前几天传播的病毒片段。

在剧院下面购买的东西是足够真实的。 Unitree 在转向两足动物之前因灵活的四足机器狗而闻名，其 G1 和 H 系列人形机器人现在已成为互联网机器人视频经济的固定装置，可以跑步、跳舞、拳击，甚至在被推挤后自己爬起来。

创始人王星星才三十多岁，持有该公司约三分之一的股份，从名义上看，他是中国第一位人形机器人亿万富翁；支持者包括腾讯、阿里巴巴和人工智能新贵 DeepSeek。

财务状况比发行外排队的人所暗示的更加微妙。 收入同比增长了四倍多，Unitree 多年来一直盈利，这对于该行业来说是不同寻常的。

然而，随着研究和营销支出的攀升，该公司第一季度净利润急剧下降，根据备案文件，净利润下降了近一半，这是一家熟悉的公司在拥挤的领域中冲刺以保持领先地位的形态，而不是靠丰厚的利润率滑行。

毫无疑问，这也是一个国家项目。 北京将人形机器人视为战略性产业，此次亮相在国内被解读为中国硬件的里程碑，而不仅仅是一次企业活动。

竞争也相应加剧，AgiBot、Leju 和 EngineAI 等竞争对手都在香港和深圳上市，而根据明显混杂的早期证据，是否有任何一家能够将病毒式示范转化为持久业务则是另一回事。

对于所有剧院来说，根本问题仍然没有解决。 Unitree 制造可以翻筋斗的机器；该公司尚未证明自己能够一头扎进大众市场，让买家保持满意，订单不断增加。

即使是英伟达（其芯片为这一繁荣提供了很大的动力）也一直在悄悄地将赌注分散到其他机器人制造商身上。 我

投资者以数千倍的价格竞购股票，押注示威活动只是序幕。 从8月19日起，市场将开始谨慎或谨慎地寻找答案。
